abstract: Abstract Neurons require mitochondrial bioenergetic flexibility to withstand chronic mitochondrial quality control failure, yet the compensatory safeguards that preserve mitochondrial functional output during neurodegenerative progression remain unclear. Here, using parkin- deficient fly models, we identify an early mitochondrial metabolic signature characterized by reduced pyruvate and increased glutamate and α-ketoglutarate. Substrate-specific mitochondrial respiration and ATP assays showed impaired pyruvate-supported bioenergetic capacity but preserved glutamate-supported bioenergetic capacity, supporting a transient glutamate-linked compensatory state before neurodegenerative deterioration. We identify neuronal TSPO upregulation as an adaptive compensatory mechanism that sustains glutamate-supported mitochondrial bioenergetic capacity under parkin -deficient conditions. In human iPSC-derived neurons, parkin deficiency was similarly associated with TSPO upregulation, and TSPO modulation altered neuronal vulnerability. TSPO induction was controlled by JNK-Jun/Nrf2 signaling, whose age-associated attenuation compromised compensation and accelerated neurodegeneration. Thus, loss of TSPO-dependent glutamate-linked bioenergetic compensation marks the transition from mitochondrial adaptation to neurodegenerative deterioration under parkin -deficient conditions.
hook: In parkin-deficient flies, TSPO upregulation sustains neuron energy until that compensation fails
summary: Parkin-deficient fly neurons lose pyruvate-fueled respiration but keep glutamate-fueled respiration, aided by higher TSPO driven by JNK-Jun/Nrf2 signaling. With age this signal fades and neurodegeneration speeds up. Human iPSC neurons showed a similar TSPO rise, but most work is in flies.
title: Failure of TSPO-dependent metabolic compensation marks the loss of mitochondrial bioenergetic adaptation in parkin-deficient neurons
